intro.html: Ordinary is not always bad: mundane chores and commonplace inventions keep life running. But when writing or speech is ordinary in a tired way, critics reach for sharper words: banal, trite, hackneyed, prosaic, pedestrian. Several of these words began as pictures: a worn coin, a hired horse, a printer’s plate, a flat plate, a walker on foot.

Ordinary: mundane (everyday), commonplace (not unusual), conventional (the usual way). Worn out by use: banal, trite, hackneyed (adjectives); cliché (an overused phrase), platitude (a flat remark offered as wisdom) (nouns). Dull and unimaginative: prosaic, pedestrian.

words.ex: Folding laundry is a {mundane} chore, so Lin listens to music while she does it.
words.ctx: The astronaut’s diary was surprisingly {mundane}: beside the views of Earth, she wrote mostly about brushing her teeth, changing air filters and what she ate for lunch.
words.etym: From Latin mundanus, “of the world,” from mundus, world: the plain, everyday world.
words.note: Mundane means ordinary, not bad: a mundane task can be pleasant enough.

mn.text: Every Monday it is the same: fold the laundry, take out the trash, wash the dishes. Plain, everyday chores like these are {mundane}.

scene.alt: A woman with headphones yawns over a basket of laundry on a Monday.

words.ex: Phones that take pictures, once a wonder, are now {commonplace}.
words.ctx: A hundred years ago, flying across the ocean was a daring adventure; today it is so {commonplace} that passengers sleep through the whole trip.
words.etym: A translation of Latin locus communis, “a common place”: a theme or saying everyone used.

mn.text: A plane roars over the river, and nobody fishing even looks up; you can see planes in common places everywhere. They are {commonplace} now.

scene.alt: A plane flies overhead while people by the river do not even look up.

words.def: following what is usually done; traditional
words.ex: Instead of a {conventional} birthday cake, Dev asked for a tower of pancakes.
words.ctx: Most builders of the time made {conventional} brick houses, but she designed homes shaped like seashells, with curving walls and round windows.
words.etym: From convention, Latin conventio, “a coming together, an agreement”: conventional ways are the ones people have agreed on.

mn.cue: CONVENTION-al: the way everyone agreed on
mn.text: At the business convention, every guest wears the same gray jacket and tie, the way everyone agreed long ago. Their style is {conventional}.

scene.alt: Three men stand in matching gray jackets and ties, while one girl in a cape stands out.

words.def: dull and unoriginal because so common
words.ex: The movie’s ending was {banal}: the hero won, the villain lost, and everyone cheered, just as we expected.
words.ctx: Hoping for a fresh insight, the class was disappointed by the speaker’s {banal} advice: “Work hard, and follow your dreams.”
words.etym: From French banal, “common to everyone,” first said of things like a village oven that everyone shared.

mn.text: Every single day, Kai’s lunch is one plain banana: no surprise, no change, nothing new. A lunch that dull and predictable is {banal}.

scene.alt: A bored boy holds up the same plain banana he has for lunch every day.

words.def: used so often that it is no longer interesting
words.ex: “Every cloud has a silver lining” felt {trite} to Maya right after she lost the match.
words.ctx: Her early poems were full of {trite} images, roses as red as fire and eyes like stars, but her later work was fresh and surprising.
words.etym: From Latin tritus, “worn,” from terere, “to rub”: a trite phrase has been rubbed smooth by use.

mn.cue: TRITE: TRIED and TRIED and TRIED
mn.text: Grandpa tells his favorite joke for the hundredth time, and the whole family groans: it has been tried too many times. The joke is {trite}.

cast.say: Ha! Did I ever tell you…

scene.alt: A grandfather tells his old joke again while the family groans.

words.ex: The {hackneyed} plot, a lost dog finds its way home, had been filmed a dozen times.
words.ctx: The judges rejected the slogan as {hackneyed}: “Better than ever” had already been printed on a thousand products.
words.etym: From hackney, an ordinary horse for hire: ridden by everyone, it was worn out with use.

mn.cue: HACKNEY: a hired horse worn out by use
mn.text: The old hired horse has carried every tourist in town and now plods along, worn out by use. An idea worn out the same way is {hackneyed}.

scene.alt: A tired old horse for hire plods along while another child waits for a ride.

words.ex: “At the end of the day” is a {cliché} that adds nothing to most sentences.
words.ctx: The story ended with a tired {cliché}: the hero woke up, and the whole adventure had been a dream.
words.etym: From French cliché, a printer’s metal plate used to stamp the same words over and over.

mn.cue: CLICK-AY: CLICK, the same stamp again
mn.text: Click! Click! Click! The old printing plate stamps the very same phrase on page after page. A phrase repeated that often is a {cliché}.

scene.alt: A printing robot stamps out page after page of the same tired phrase while a girl yawns.

words.def: a dull, obvious remark offered as if it were wise or new
words.ex: “Everything happens for a reason” was the only {platitude} the coach could offer after the loss.
words.ctx: Instead of real advice, the speaker offered {platitudes}: “Believe in yourself,” “Never give up” and “Tomorrow is another day.”
words.etym: From French platitude, “flatness,” from plat, flat: a platitude is a flat, dull remark.

mn.text: Uncle Victor serves up an empty plate of wisdom: “Well, it is what it is.” A flat, obvious remark offered as if it were deep is a {platitude}.

scene.alt: A man proudly offers an empty plate along with an obvious saying; a teen is unimpressed.

words.ex: Asked what the clouds looked like, the {prosaic} boy said only, “Clouds.”
words.ctx: Visitors expected the castle to hide secret passages and treasure, but its history was {prosaic}: for three hundred years it had mostly stored grain.
words.etym: From Latin prosaicus, from prosa, prose: plain, ordinary writing, as opposed to poetry.

mn.text: Zoe looks up and sees a dragon, a castle and a ship in the clouds. Sami looks up and says, “Those are clouds.” His plain, unpoetic answer is {prosaic}.

scene.alt: A girl sees a dragon in the clouds; the boy beside her just sees clouds.

words.ex: The band’s second album was {pedestrian} compared with its brilliant first one.
words.ctx: The menu promised adventure, but the food was {pedestrian}: plain noodles, plain chicken and a salad anyone could make at home.
words.etym: From Latin pedester, “on foot,” from pes, foot: writing that plods along on foot, never taking flight, is pedestrian.
words.note: As a noun, a pedestrian is a person walking. As an adjective, pedestrian usually means dull, not “on foot.”

mn.cue: PED = FOOT: plods along, never flies
mn.text: Jonah’s story plods along like a tired walker, step, step, step, with a snail for company. Writing that never takes flight is {pedestrian}.

scene.alt: A bored teen plods down the sidewalk beside a slow snail.

head: word
part of speech
what is ordinary about it
rows: an overused phrase; a flat remark posing as wisdom

after.html: Many of these words began as pictures: trite (rubbed smooth, like a worn coin), hackneyed (a hired horse), cliché (a printer’s stamp), platitude (flatness), pedestrian (on foot). Remembering the picture helps you remember the meaning.

items.q: A critic calls a new novel’s writing pedestrian. What does she mean?
choices: It is about people who walk.
It moves at a quick pace.
items.why: As an adjective, pedestrian means ordinary and dull. The noun pedestrian (a walker) is a different use.

items.q: True or false: calling a task mundane means it is harmful or wrong.
items.why: False. Mundane means ordinary and everyday, not bad.

items.q: “Well, you win some, you lose some,” said Grandpa, as if it were deep wisdom. His remark was a…
items.why: A dull, obvious remark offered as if it were wise is a platitude.

items.q: Which word is closest in meaning to hackneyed?
items.why: Hackneyed and trite both mean worn out by overuse. Conventional means following the usual way; mundane and commonplace mean ordinary, not overused.
